summary:
Margin Zero is a cooperative space mission design game for one or two players. You run a nearly bankrupt space agency: choose a contract, then design a rocket under a tight budget, trading off mass, thrust, fuel, power, thermal protection and part quality. A pre-launch checklist shows whether the design can lift off, reach its destination and survive the conditions there. Then you fly the mission yourself: launch, orbital transfer, re-entry and landing, while solar flares, micrometeoroids and failing parts force quick decisions. Every flight ends with a debrief that breaks down the result: landing grade, deadline, damage and payout.

It addresses the challenge by turning the whole mission life cycle, from concept to operation, into one connected system instead of isolated lessons. Every decision has a consequence later in the flight, there is no single perfect design, and lost ships teach lessons that carry into the next attempt. Physics and hazards are modeled on NASA and JPL open data.

This matters because students rarely get to experiment with a complete mission. Margin Zero makes those trade-offs concrete and playable, building systems thinking, teamwork and interest in space engineering.
details:
What it does
Margin Zero is a roguelite space mission game for one or two players. Each run is a contract: accept a delivery to a moon or planet, design a rocket on a limited budget, launch it, fly it across the system, land it and collect the payout. Credits, spare parts, insurance and lessons learned persist between runs.

How it works
The mission is one continuous chain of six phases: Contract, Build, Launch, Fly, Land and Debrief.

  • Contract: each offer shows payout, deadline, estimated delta-v and danger rumors. Players also choose an insurance level.
  • Build: players stack engines, tanks, decouplers, heat shields, parachutes, landing legs, solar panels, radiators and computers. Each part comes in four qualities (scrap, used, new, mystery) with a price and a hidden condition. A live checklist verifies thrust-to-weight, delta-v, power, and heat and cold tolerance for the chosen destination.
  • Launch, Fly, Land: players time ignition, throttle through Max-Q, stage, burn in orbit under simulated gravity, hold an entry corridor, and deploy parachutes or brake with engines. Parts can fail under stress, and solar flares or micrometeoroids open event cards where players choose between options with different odds and costs.
  • Debrief: the result is broken down line by line: landing grade, deadline, losses and payout.

In two-player mode, one player commands and pilots while the other walks through the ship as a crew member and repairs failures.

Benefits and intended impact
Students experience a whole mission as one system instead of isolated topics. A cheap tank, a missing radiator or a steep entry angle has visible consequences minutes later, so players learn why trade-offs matter. Failure is part of learning: lost ships unlock lessons for the next attempt. We want classrooms, clubs and outreach events to use it as a first hands-on contact with mission design.

What we hope to achieve
A game that is fun first and teaches systems thinking as a side effect, and that grows with more destinations, real mission scenarios and classroom materials.

Tools
Godot Engine 4.7 and GDScript; a pure simulation layer (rocket equation, gravity, thermal balance, failure odds) covered by automated headless tests; our own pixel art; procedural sound synthesis; Exo 2 and Space Mono typefaces (SIL Open Font License); Git and GitHub. NASA and JPL open data informed the physics and hazards.

Creativity
Instead of a spreadsheet-style simulator, the mission is framed as running a nearly bankrupt agency. Risk is a game mechanic: hidden part flaws, fogged odds, insurance, side bets and win streaks make engineering margins something players feel.

Factors we considered
Accessibility for beginners (per-phase tutorials, an assisted mode, a reduced-motion option), short sessions, replayability, physical plausibility over exact realism, cooperative play on one keyboard and gamepad, and a scope we could finish during the hackathon.

Use of Artificial Intelligence
We used AI tools as assistants. The team defined the game design, reviewed and tested every result, and is responsible for the final project.

  • Code and tests: Claude Code (Anthropic) and Cursor helped write, refactor and debug GDScript, Python tools and automated tests. The Godot AI plugin (an MCP server) let these assistants operate the Godot editor and run the tests. AI co-authored commits are labeled as such in the repository history.
  • Design documents and data: AI assistants helped draft and organize our design and research documents, and helped structure the planetary data table taken from the NASA NSSDCA Planetary Fact Sheet. The team reviewed them.
  • Art: We used ArtCraft and VectorCraft to design the visual identity and art concepts (logo, rocket variants, planets and backgrounds). The in-game pixel art and UI mockups are generated procedurally by our own Python scripts and Godot shaders, written with AI coding assistance.
  • Music and sound: The soundtrack tracks and stems were generated with ElevenLabs Music, and the audio files keep ElevenLabs’ embedded content-credentials (C2PA) metadata. Sound effects are synthesized in real time by our own GDScript code.
  • Demo video: Recorded from real gameplay captures. The script, editing and subtitles were produced with Claude (Anthropic). The narration is a synthetic text-to-speech voice (Microsoft Zira), and the background music is one of the ElevenLabs tracks.
  • Submission texts: The project summary and details were drafted with Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team.
